'''Nicolaas Bloembergen''' (March 11, 1920 – September 5, 2017) was a Dutch–American [[physicist]] recognized for his work in developing driving principles behind [[nonlinear optics]] for [[laser spectroscopy]].<ref name="death">{{cite web|url=https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/nieuws/2017/09/nobelprijswinnaar-nicolaas-bloembergen-97-overleden|title=Nobelprijswinnaar Nicolaas Bloembergen (97) overleden|website=Universiteit Leiden|date=September 6, 2017 |access-date=May 3, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=http://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20170908071727/https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/nieuws/2017/09/nobelprijswinnaar-nicolaas-bloembergen-97-overleden|archive-date=September 8, 2017}}</ref> During his career, he was a professor at [[Harvard University]] and later at the [[University of Arizona]] and at Leiden University in 1973 (as Lorentz Professor).

Bloembergen shared the 1981 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] along with [[Arthur Schawlow]] and [[Kai Siegbahn]] because their work "has had a profound effect on our present knowledge of the constitution of matter" through the use of [[laser spectroscopy]]. In particular, Bloembergen was singled out because he "founded a new field of science we now call [[non-linear optics]]" by mixing "two or more beams of laser light... in order to produce laser light of a different wave length" and thus significantly broaden the laser spectroscopy frequency band.<ref name="Nobel"/>

== Education ==
Nicolaas Bloembergen was born on March 11, 1920, in [[Dordrecht]], Netherlands, where his father was a chemical engineer and executive.<ref name="Nobel">Nobel Foundation [https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1981/ceremony-speech/ 1981 Nobel Presentation Speech by Professor Ingvar Lindgren] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011080049/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1981/bloembergen-autobio.html |date=October 11, 2007 }}</ref> He had five siblings, with his brother [[Auke Bloembergen|Auke]] later becoming a legal scholar.<ref name=histor>{{cite web |author=Rob Herber |url=http://historischekringdebilt.nl/wp-content/uploads/DBG-Nico-Bloembergen-fysicus-in-licht.pdf |title=Nico Bloembergen, fysicus in licht |language=nl |publisher=Historische Kring De Bilt |access-date=June 18, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012210545/http://historischekringdebilt.nl/wp-content/uploads/DBG-Nico-Bloembergen-fysicus-in-licht.pdf |archive-date=October 12, 2016 }}</ref> Bloembergen entered [[Utrecht University]] in 1938 to study physics, receiving his [[Candidate of Philosophy|C.Phil.]] in 1941 and his ''[[doctorandus]]'' in 1943.<ref name=Arizona>{{Cite web|title=Nicolaas Bloembergen|url=http://www.optics.arizona.edu/research/faculty/profile/nicolaas-bloembergen|url-status=dead|publisher=[[University of Arizona]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017120935/http://www.optics.arizona.edu/research/faculty/profile/nicolaas-bloembergen|archive-date=2013-10-17|access-date=2016-03-26}}</ref> In 1943, during the German occupation of the Netherlands, the German authorities closed the University and Bloembergen spent two years in hiding.<ref name="Nobel"/>

Bloembergen left the war-ravaged Netherlands in 1945 to pursue graduate studies at [[Harvard University]] under Professor [[Edward Mills Purcell]].<ref name="EMP">{{cite book|url=https://www.nap.edu/read/9977/chapter/12|title=Edward Mills Purcell|year=2000 |publisher=NAP.edu|doi=10.17226/9977 |isbn=978-0-309-07035-5 |access-date=September 6, 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907075314/https://www.nap.edu/read/9977/chapter/12|archive-date=September 7, 2017}}</ref> Through Purcell, Bloembergen was part of the prolific academic lineage tree of [[J. J. Thomson]], which includes many other Nobel Laureates, beginning with Thomson himself (Physics Nobel, 1906) and [[John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh|Lord Rayleigh]] (Physics Nobel, 1904), [[Ernest Rutherford]] (Chemistry Nobel 1908), [[Owen Richardson]] (Physics Nobel, 1928), and finally Purcell (Physics, Nobel 1952). Bloembergen's other influences include [[John Van Vleck]] (Physics Nobel, 1977) and [[Percy Bridgman]] (Physics Nobel, 1946).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/units/fhp/newsletters/spring2011/huber.cfm|title=John Van Vleck: Quantum Theory and Magnetism|author=David L. Hubber|publisher=APS.org|access-date=September 6, 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907033522/https://www.aps.org/units/fhp/newsletters/spring2011/huber.cfm|archive-date=September 7, 2017}}</ref>

Six weeks before his arrival, Purcell and his graduate students Torrey and Pound discovered [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR).<ref name="EMP"/> Bloembergen was hired to develop the first NMR machine. At Harvard he attended lectures by [[Julian Schwinger|Schwinger]], [[John Hasbrouck Van Vleck|Van Vleck]], and [[Edwin C. Kemble|Kemble]].<ref name="Nobel"/> Bloembergen's NMR systems are the predecessors of modern-day [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]] machines, which are used to examine internal organs and tissues.<ref name="UUS"/> Bloembergen's research on NMR led to an interest in [[maser]]s, which were introduced in 1953 and are the predecessors of [[laser]]s.<ref name="Medi">{{cite web|url=http://www.mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/bloembergen|title=Nicolaas Bloembergen|publisher=Mediatheque|access-date=September 6, 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907040053/http://www.mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/bloembergen|archive-date=September 7, 2017}}</ref>

Bloembergen returned to the Netherlands in 1947, and submitted his doctoral thesis, ''Nuclear Magnetic Relaxation'', at [[Leiden University]].<ref name="NMR">{{cite journal |author=Nicolaas Bloembergen |author2=Edward Mills Purcell |author-link2=Edward Mills Purcell |author3=Robert V. Pound |author-link3=Robert Pound |url=http://redeye.mmrrcc.upenn.edu/mediawiki/images/8/89/A13.pdf |title=Relaxation effects in nuclear magnetic resonance absorption |journal=Physical Review |volume=73 |issue=7 |pages=679 |date=1948 |bibcode=1948PhRv...73..679B |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.73.679 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100624181140/http://redeye.mmrrcc.upenn.edu/mediawiki/images/8/89/A13.pdf |archive-date=June 24, 2010 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This was because he had completed all the preliminary  examinations in the Netherlands, and [[Cornelis Jacobus Gorter]] of Leiden offered him a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral]] appointment there.<ref name="NMR"/> He received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from Leiden in 1948, and then was a postdoc at Leiden for about a year.<ref name="Nobel"/>

== Career ==
In 1949, Bloembergen returned to Harvard as a junior fellow of the [[Harvard Society of Fellows|Society of Fellows]]. In 1951, he became an associate professor; he then became Gordon McKay Professor of Applied Physics in 1957; [[Rumford Chair of Physics|Rumford Professor of Physics]] in 1974; and Gerhard Gade University Professor in 1980.<ref name="IEEE">{{cite web |url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Nicolaas_Bloembergen |title=Nicolaas Bloembergen |work=IEEE Global History Network |publisher=IEEE |access-date=July 18, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120409051228/http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Nicolaas_Bloembergen |archive-date=April 9, 2012 }}</ref> He retired from Harvard in 1990.<ref name="IEEE"/>

In addition, Bloembergen served as a visiting professor. From 1964 to 1965, Bloembergen was a visiting professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="Nobel"/> In 1996–1997, he was a visiting scientist in the Optical Sciences Center at the [[University of Arizona]]; he became a professor at Arizona in 2001.<ref name=Arizona/> Bloembergen was a member of the board of sponsors of the ''[http://www.thebulletin.org Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]'' and honorary editor of the ''[[Journal of Nonlinear Optical Physics & Materials]]''.<ref>World Scientific. ''Journal of Nonlinear Optical Physics & Materials''. [http://www.worldscientific.com/page/jnopm/editorial-board ''Journal Editorial Board''].</ref>

== Research ==
By 1960 while at Harvard, Bloembergen experimented with [[microwave spectroscope|microwave spectroscopy]].<ref name="Medi"/> He had modified the [[maser]] of [[Charles Townes]],<ref name="Laser">{{cite web|url=https://www.pddnet.com/news/2016/03/today-engineering-history-laser-patented|title=Today in Engineering History: The Laser Is Patented|work=Product Design and Development |date=March 22, 2016|access-date=September 6, 2017|publisher=PDDNet|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907034554/https://www.pddnet.com/news/2016/03/today-engineering-history-laser-patented|archive-date=September 7, 2017}}</ref> and in 1956, he developed a crystal maser, which was more powerful than the standard gaseous version.<ref name="NMR"/>

With the advent of the laser, Bloembergen participated in the development of the field of [[laser spectroscopy]], which allows precise observations of atomic structure using lasers. Following the development of [[second-harmonic generation]] by [[Peter Franken]] and others in 1961, Bloembergen studied how a new structure of matter is revealed, when one bombards [[matter]] with a focused and high-intensity beam of [[photons]]. This he termed the study of [[nonlinear optics]]. In reflection to his work in a Dutch newspaper in 1990, Bloembergen said: "We took a standard textbook on optics and for each section we asked ourselves what would happen if the intensity was to become very high. We were almost certain that we were bound to encounter an entirely new type of physics within that domain".<ref name="UUS">{{cite web|url=https://www.uu.nl/en/research/nicolaas-bloembergen|publisher=[[Utrecht University]]|title=Nicolaas Bloembergen|access-date=September 6, 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907033725/https://www.uu.nl/en/research/nicolaas-bloembergen|archive-date=September 7, 2017}}</ref>

From this theoretical work, Bloembergen found ways to combine two or more laser sources consisting of photons in the [[light|visible light frequency range]] to generate a single laser source with photons of different frequencies in the [[infrared]] and [[ultraviolet]] ranges, which extends the amount of atomic detail that can be gathered from laser spectroscopy.<ref name="Medi"/>

== Personal life and death ==
Bloembergen met Huberta Deliana "Deli" Brink in 1948 while on vacation with his university's Physics Club. She was able to travel with him to the United States in 1949 on a student hospitality exchange program; he proposed to her when they arrived in the States, and were married by 1950 on return to Amsterdam.<ref name="nobel bio"/> They both became [[naturalization|naturalized]] U.S. citizens in 1958.<ref name="IEEE"/> They had three children.<ref name="nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=Nicolaas Bloembergen – Biographical|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1981/bloembergen/biographical/|url-status=live|publisher=[[Nobel Foundation]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171212002420/https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1981/bloembergen-bio.html|archive-date=2017-12-12|access-date=2017-09-06}}</ref>

Bloembergen died on September 5, 2017, at an assisted living facility in his hometown [[Tucson, Arizona]], of cardiorespiratory failure at the age of 97.<ref>{{cite == Legacy ==
On March 11, 2020, the day of Bloembergen's 100th birthday, a team of researchers at the [[University of New South Wales]] published an article in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', demonstrating for the first time the successful coherent control of the nucleus of a single atom using only electric fields, an idea first proposed by Bloembergen back in 1961.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Asaad|first1=Serwan|last2=Mourik|first2=Vincent|last3=Joecker|first3=Benjamin|last4=Johnson|first4=Mark A. I.|last5=Baczewski|first5=Andrew D.|last6=Firgau|first6=Hannes R.|last7=Mądzik|first7=Mateusz T.|last8=Schmitt|first8=Vivien|last9=Pla|first9=Jarryd J.|last10=Hudson|first10=Fay E.|last11=Itoh|first11=Kohei M.|date=March 2020|title=Coherent electrical control of a single high-spin nucleus in silicon|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2057-7|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=579|issue=7798|pages=205–209|doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2057-7|pmid=32161384|issn=1476-4687|arxiv=1906.01086|bibcode=2020Natur.579..205A|s2cid=174797899}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Science|first=American Association for the Advancement of|date=April 28, 1961|title=National Academy of Sciences: Abstracts of Papers Presented at the Annual Meeting, 24-26 April 1961, Washington, D.C.|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.133.3461.1363|journal=Science|language=en|volume=133|issue=3461|pages=1363–1370|doi=10.1126/science.133.3461.1363|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17744956|bibcode=1961Sci...133.1363.|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=How an Accident Sparked a Quantum Computing Breakthrough|url=https://www.seeker.com/videos/space-innovation/how-an-accident-sparked-a-quantum-computing-breakthrough|last=Seeker|website=Seeker|date=May 11, 2020 |access-date=May 13, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=This Accidently &#91;sic&#93; Solved Puzzle Can Help Make Powerful Quantum Computers|url=https://analyticsindiamag.com/this-accidently-solved-puzzle-can-help-make-powerful-quantum-computers/|last=Yadav|first=Rohit|date=April 10, 2020|website=Analytics India Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=May 13, 2020}}</ref>
